meta.title: The First 90 Days
meta.subtitle: Scenario 47 — The First Night (a fictional composite)
meta.summary: You are Renata. Your sitter canceled, your shift did not, and your seven-year-old was home alone for part of one evening. Tonight a caseworker is deciding where Ines sleeps — and whether the first name the file ever holds is your sister's.

nodes.title: 6:40 p.m.
body: Your sitter's text came at 6:12, while you were already on the bus to the diner: her car died, she cannot come. Ines is seven. She has been alone before for twenty minutes while you ran to the corner store, never for a whole shift, and you told yourself the whole ride that the neighbor upstairs would check in — she always does at seven.

At 6:40 there is a knock that is not Mrs. Halloway's. A county caseworker, Ms. Krajewski, stands with a police officer and explains, evenly, that a caller reported a child alone in the apartment. Ines is on the couch with her tablet, fed, unhurt, and frightened mostly by the uniforms.

choices.text: Cooperate. Let them in, answer plainly, and say nothing you would not want written down.

nodes.title: The checklist
body: Ms. Krajewski works through a form on a tablet: who lives here, who watches Ines, Ines's school, her doctor. The questions are ordinary. The tablet is not. Everything you say is becoming the first page of a file that will outlive this night, and it will be quoted back at you in rooms you have not seen yet.
She asks the question the form saves for last: "Is there a relative or another adult Ines knows well — someone she could stay with tonight, if it comes to that?"

choices.text: Answer it in full — out loud and in writing on her form: "My sister, Yolanda Reyes. She lives ten minutes away. Ines stays with her every other weekend. Here is her number — write it exactly like this."
Answer out loud, carefully: "My sister Yolanda. She is close with Ines." You assume the tablet caught it.

nodes.title: What the tablet caught
body: Ms. Krajewski nods and keeps typing. What the form will actually hold, you cannot see from where you stand — and a name spoken in a doorway at night has a way of becoming, in the file, "mother states sister may be available." No number. No address. Nobody will fault the worker; the night is full of doorways.
You can still fix it before she leaves — if you think of it.

choices.text: Ask her to add the number and address to the form now, and to read back what the form says about your sister.
Let it stand. She said she would note it, and tonight is not the night to argue with the person holding the pen.

nodes.title: Ink, not air
body: Ms. Krajewski reads it back: Yolanda Reyes, address, phone, "maternal aunt; child stays with her regularly; mother requests aunt be contacted first." It is eleven words longer than a name spoken aloud, and it is the eleven words that will still exist on Thursday.
Names in a file get called. Names in the air get remembered, sometimes.

choices.text: Thank her, and ask what happens next, step by step.

nodes.title: The decision
body: The decision comes inside the hour, and it is not the one you prayed for: Ines cannot stay here tonight. The county is taking emergency custody, and a judge will review it at a shelter care hearing that must happen within 72 hours — by Thursday. The law behind that clock is 23 Pa.C.S. § 6315(d) and 42 Pa.C.S. § 6332, though tonight nobody says the citations out loud.
Where Ines sleeps until Thursday is a separate question from whether she had to leave — and it is the question your next hour is about.

choices.text: Ask it plainly: "Before any foster home — will you call my sister tonight?"

nodes.title: The call
body: Ms. Krajewski calls Yolanda from your kitchen table. Yolanda answers on the second ring, and does not hesitate: "Tell me what she needs. I am coming." What Yolanda cannot do tonight is pass, on the spot, every check the county runs before a child sleeps in a kinship home — some of those checks simply take days, and a Tuesday night cannot be argued into a Thursday.
Ines will sleep tonight in an emergency foster home, with a kind stranger named Mrs. Halloway. The fight is not about tonight anymore. It is about Thursday — and about what is ready by then.

choices.text: Pack Ines's bag yourself: her blanket, her school clothes, the stuffed fox. Put Yolanda's number in the front pocket, on paper.

nodes.title: The bag
body: You pack like a woman who has done it for weekends at her sister's, because you have. Ines holds the fox and asks if Aunt Yo's couch bed counts as a sleepover. You say: Thursday, baby. First a judge listens, then sleepovers.

Ms. Krajewski gives you a paper with a court date and a name you do not recognize — and one instruction worth more than the paper: "Call the public defender's office in the morning. You are entitled to a lawyer."

choices.text: Write Yolanda's number on the back of the court paper too. Paper goes where you go.

nodes.title: The public defender's office
body: Ms. Fontaine, the attorney the court appoints for you, has the file's first pages before you sit down. The right is not a favor: in a dependency case you are entitled to counsel — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6337 guarantees it for parents, and § 6332(a) does the same at the shelter care stage. Ms. Fontaine reads the doorway page twice.
"Thursday is a shelter care hearing," she says. "The judge decides whether Ines stays in care at all — and if she does, where. The where is a real question at shelter care, not a detail for later."

choices.text: "Then where is my whole case. What does the judge need to see by Thursday?"

nodes.title: What the judge needs
body: "Three things," Ms. Fontaine says. "Your sister, in the courtroom or on the phone, saying yes out loud. Whatever checks the agency can finish by Thursday, finished — which means your sister calls them tomorrow morning, not the other way around. And a childcare plan from you that is not 'it won't happen again' — names, shifts, backups. Judges place children with plans, not promises."
She slides a card across the desk: the agency's records office. "And one more thing. You may ask for your record. Parents ask; agencies produce. Ask early."

choices.text: Call Yolanda before you leave the office. Put her on the phone with Ms. Fontaine.
Take the card and go home to think. Thursday feels far away.

nodes.title: Thinking
body: Home is quiet in the wrong way. Ines's cup is still in the sink. You think for an evening, and the thinking costs a day — the checks that could have started Wednesday morning will now start Wednesday afternoon, and Thursday does not move for anybody.
By Wednesday you are doing everything on Ms. Fontaine's list anyway. You are just doing it a day poorer.

choices.text: Do the list. All of it, a day late.

nodes.title: Yolanda goes first
body: Yolanda does not wait to be found. She calls the agency Wednesday morning, gives her clearances information, opens her door for a walk-through that afternoon, and says the sentence kinship runs on: "She has a bed here. She has always had a bed here." The walk-through notes a home that a seven-year-old already knows — her toothbrush is in the bathroom.
Ms. Fontaine files a one-page request ahead of the hearing: if care continues, placement with the maternal aunt — the relative named in the file from the first night.

choices.text: Spend Wednesday evening writing your childcare plan: the sitter, the backup sitter, Yolanda, and your manager's letter about the shift swap.

nodes.title: The plan, on paper
body: It takes two pages. Primary sitter, with a phone number. Backup: the neighbor on the third floor, asked and agreed, in writing. Yolanda as emergency contact for any gap longer than an hour. And your manager's letter: your Tuesday and Thursday shifts move to daytime for ninety days, signed.
It is not an apology. It is better than an apology. It is a system.

choices.text: Give a copy to Ms. Fontaine. Keep the original.

nodes.title: One more envelope
body: Ms. Fontaine asks if you want the agency's record started toward you now. "Pennsylvania's regulation gives a parent the right to ask for their child's and their own case record in writing — 55 Pa. Code § 3130.44(d). What Thursday decides will be written down. You should be able to read what was written."
The request takes four lines and a stamp.

choices.text: Sign it and mail it today.
Skip it. Thursday is the fight; paper can wait.

nodes.title: Thursday
body: The courtroom is small and the clock on the wall is loud. Ms. Krajewski testifies first: a child alone, a sitter who canceled, a mother who cooperated. Then Ms. Fontaine presents the plan, the manager's letter — and calls on Yolanda, sitting in the second row with her clearance paperwork in a folder on her knees.
The judge looks at the agency. "Counsel, the aunt. Where are we?"

choices.text: Listen. This is the moment the first night built — or didn't.

nodes.title: The question
body: Everything since Monday narrows to what the file can prove about your sister: whether she was named early enough to be checked, engaged enough to be ready, and standing close enough to be heard. The judge turns the pages of the doorway form.
What happens next is decided by what is actually in front of her.

choices.text: The file names Yolanda from the first night, with her number — and she is here, checks underway, asking to be heard about taking Ines tonight.
The file is thinner than that — a sister mentioned, a study barely begun.

nodes.title: Ending — Home by Thursday
debrief: The judge continues Ines's care — the night alone was real, and no judge waves it away — but orders her placed with Yolanda tonight, with the kinship approval to be completed on a date the court sets and says out loud. Ines's sleepover ruling comes with rules: your plan governs, your shifts are day shifts, and any childcare gap goes to the names on your two pages, in order.

You have won the outcome this scenario exists to teach: in an emergency, the placement fight is won or lost in the first hours. The law gave you the clock — a shelter care hearing within 72 hours (42 Pa.C.S. § 6332; 23 Pa.C.S. § 6315(d)) and a lawyer to stand with you (42 Pa.C.S. § 6337; § 6332(a)). The rest was sequence: the relative named in writing at the door, the relative who called the agency before the agency called her, and a plan with names in it. Caseworkers change; the first page of the file does not.

What no strategy controls: the judge. A different judge could have kept Ines in the foster home until the aunt's approval was complete, on the same papers. What the early naming bought was not a guarantee — it bought the question being asked at all, on Thursday instead of next month.

nodes.title: Ending — Named Too Late (partial)
debrief: The judge continues Ines's care and keeps her with Mrs. Halloway for now — kindly, and with a date: the aunt's study is ordered opened, kinship placement to be revisited at a review in ten days if the checks are complete. It is not a loss. It is the same road, walked ten days longer, with a seven-year-old sleeping at a stranger's in between.

Read the debrief honestly: nothing about Yolanda changed between the two endings. Her house, her heart, and her toothbrush were identical. What changed was when the file learned her name in a form the system could act on — a name spoken in a doorway became "may be available," and maybes do not get clearance appointments. The shelter care clock (within 72 hours — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6332; 23 Pa.C.S. § 6315(d)) protects the hearing. It does not protect the placement. That part is yours, and it starts at the door.

This ending is a partial win, and it is recoverable: the study is open, the date is real, and the record — which you can request in writing under 55 Pa. Code § 3130.44(d) — will carry your sister's name correctly from here. Parents reach the kinship ending from here all the time. They just reach it later than the first night allowed.
